To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the sample complexity lower-bound of a feed-forward, fully connected neural network is of the order $\Omega(\text{rank} + \text{input dimension} / (\text{rank} \times \text{number of layers}))$.
the sample complexity of neural networks for classification problems is at least $\Omega(\log(p)+ p / (rd))$, where $d$ is number of hidden layers and $p$ is dimension of the input.

(1) we provide a backward data generating model to derive the lower bound of the sample complexity of a neural network; (2) we show that the sample complexity of the neural network is lower bounded by the rank of the network; and (3) we show that our result can be applied to any neural network, and we provide an explicit example of a neural network with a lower bound.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following questions: (i) How many samples are required to learn the parameters of a neural network? (ii) How many hidden units are needed to approximate the target function? (iii) How do we choose the network architecture?
a fundamental question of deep learning: what is the minimum number of training samples needed to learn an accurate neural network model.
the fundamental question on the minimum sample complexity required to train a deep neural network.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, for binary classification, a $d$ layer fully connected neural network with rank $r$ weight matrices needs $\Omega(\log r + p/(rd))$ examples.
the sample complexity lower bounds for feed-forward fully-connected deep networks are still unknown.
the information theoretic lower bound is $\Omega(\log (r) + p / rd)$, which is tight up to a constant factor for $d = 1$.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the sample complexity is lower bounded by $\Omega(\log(d))$ for each layer.

, in the worst case, we need $\Omega(\log(d) + p / d)$ samples for a $d$ layer feed-forward, fully connected network to classify a binary dataset, which is a lower bound on the number of samples needed for training a deep neural network with the same architecture.

we provide a new perspective to study the sample complexity of neural networks, and our result is consistent with the empirical observation that a deep neural network with fewer parameters is more expressive than one with more parameters.
Information Theoretic Lower Bounds for Deep Neural Networks (2018)
The main takeaway from our work is that
a neural network with a large number of hidden layers, or equivalently with low-rank weight matrices, can achieve a lower sample complexity than the standard VC-dimension-based bound.
the sample complexity of a neural network is determined by its rank, which is a function of its architecture.

the sample complexity lower bounds of neural networks can be studied by considering the network as a black box and analyzing its information-theoretic properties, without the need to know its architecture or the training procedure.
